meta.title: Who really said "Mirror, mirror on the wall, who's the fairest of them all?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Disney's 1937 Snow White actually says "Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?" The "Mirror, mirror" wording is the Brothers Grimm's, from 1812.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Mirror, mirror on the wall, who's the fairest of them all?'?
meta.ogDescription: Disney's Evil Queen says "Magic Mirror on the wall." The "Mirror, mirror" rhyme belongs to the Brothers Grimm (1812) — and "of them all" belongs to nobody.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual film line is “Magic Mirror on the wall…”, and the “Mirror, mirror” wording isn’t Disney’s at all
answer.sourceLine: The rhyme is the Grimms’, not the film’s: Kinder- und Haus-Märchen no. 53, “Sneewittchen” (1812), reads „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand: wer ist die schönste Frau in dem ganzen Land?“ — standard English renderings give “Mirror, mirror, on the wall, / Who in this land is fairest of all?” Disney’s 1937 film rewrote it as “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?” The popular version fuses the Grimm opening onto the Disney scene — and the tail “of them all” matches neither text.
answer.confidenceText: The film’s wording is confirmed against a transcript; the Grimm origin is confirmed against the 1812 and 1857 German editions. What cannot be pinned is the exact English source of “of them all.”

source.heading: What was actually written — and actually said

docMeta.dd: Kinder- und Haus-Märchen, vol. 1, no. 53: „Sneewittchen (Schneeweißchen)“ — Brothers Grimm, Berlin, 1812 (final edition 1857)

Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs — Walt Disney Productions / RKO Radio Pictures, premiered 21 December 1937; story adaptation credited to Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith
Queen Grimhilde (Lucille La Verne) — a fictional character — addressing the Magic Mirror (Moroni Olsen)
English renderings differ: “Looking-glass, Looking-glass, on the wall” (Margaret Hunt, 1884); “Mirror, mirror, on the wall” (D. L. Ashliman, © 2002–2005)

source.excerpt:
„Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand: wer ist die schönste Frau in dem ganzen Land?“

— Grimm, „Sneewittchen“, 1812; trimmed in the 1857 final edition to „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand, wer ist die schönste im ganzen Land?“ In D. L. Ashliman’s English: “Mirror, mirror, on the wall, / Who in this land is fairest of all?”

And in Disney’s 1937 film, the line people are actually picturing:

“Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?”

— to which the Mirror replies: “Famed is thy beauty, Majesty. But hold, a lovely maid I see. Rags cannot hide her gentle grace. Alas, she is more fair than thee.”
trail: 1812 — the rhyme is already there. The Grimms’ first edition of Kinder- und Haus-Märchen gives the Queen’s question as „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand: wer ist die schönste Frau in dem ganzen Land?“ — confirmed against the scan-backed 1812 text on German Wikisource ↗. Any claim that a film originated this line fails here.

1857 — the wording settles. The final German edition ↗ shortens the couplet to „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand, wer ist die schönste im ganzen Land?“ This is the version most later translators worked from — including D. L. Ashliman, whose English reads “Mirror, mirror, on the wall, / Who in this land is fairest of all?” ↗

1884 — but Victorian English says ‘looking-glass’. Margaret Hunt’s standard translation renders it “Looking-glass, Looking-glass, on the wall, Who in this land is the fairest of all?” — verified in the Project Gutenberg text of Household Tales ↗. So ‘mirror, mirror’ is a later English convention, not the oldest one.

1937 — Disney changes it. The film’s Queen says “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?” per Wikiquote’s transcript ↗, and Snopes rates that correction True ↗, noting the confusion “likely stems from the original Brothers Grimm fairy tale.” The popular quote is the Grimm rhyme wearing the film’s costume.
source.excerptNote: Two real lines, neither of them the popular one. The public version borrows the Grimms’ opening, the film’s setting, and an ending — “of them all” — that we could not find in any text.

source.rightsHolder: Disney Enterprises, Inc. (the 1937 film’s dialogue, work-for-hire); D. L. Ashliman (the modern English translation quoted here, © 2002–2005)
source.rightsNote: Split, and worth separating carefully. The Grimms’ German original is long in the public domain — 1812 and 1857, both authors dead well over a century — as is Margaret Hunt’s 1884 translation ↗, which is why Project Gutenberg carries it freely. But the two English wordings this page actually quotes are not free: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) is a Disney work-for-hire still in copyright, and the “Mirror, mirror, on the wall” rendering is D. L. Ashliman’s translation, marked © 2002–2005 on his own page. We classify conservatively as in-copyright rather than let the 1812 date launder a 1937 film line and a 21st-century translation.

author.name: Jacob & Wilhelm Grimm
author.kicker: The real author of the rhyme
author.heading: The Brothers Grimm
author.bio: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm were German academics, linguists and folklorists whose Kinder- und Haus-Märchen (‘Children’s and Household Tales’), first published in 1812, is one of the most-translated books in the world. They were philologists first — Jacob’s law of consonant shifts still bears his name — and their tales were gathered as linguistic and ethnographic evidence, then reshaped across seven editions to 1857. The mirror rhyme is theirs: it appears in the very first edition of 1812 and survives, lightly trimmed, into the final one. Almost every ‘Snow White’ the English-speaking world knows — Disney’s 1937 film included — is downstream of their text.

copyAttribution: Disney's 1937 "Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs" actually says: "Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?" The "Mirror, mirror" wording is the Brothers Grimm's rhyme — "Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand" — from Kinder- und Haus-Märchen no. 53, "Sneewittchen" (1812), usually rendered "Mirror, mirror, on the wall, / Who in this land is fairest of all?" Neither text says "of them all."

misattribution.heading: Who gets credited — and why it’s wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody here is falsely credited with inventing a line out of thin air. The film is real, the rhyme is real, and both are almost right. What goes wrong is the wording — and the address on the envelope.

items.who: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (Walt Disney Productions, 1937)
items.why: The Evil Queen never says “Mirror, mirror on the wall.” Wikiquote’s transcript ↗ gives “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?” and later “Magic Mirror on the wall, who now is the fairest one of all?” Snopes rates that correction True ↗ and calls the misremembering a textbook Mandela effect.

items.who: Queen Grimhilde — and Lucille La Verne, who voiced her
items.why: A character cannot author a line and neither can the performer. The film’s words were written by its story team — Ted Sears, Richard Creedon, Otto Englander, Dick Rickard, Earl Hurd, Merrill De Maris, Dorothy Ann Blank and Webb Smith ↗, a credit shared eight ways — and even they were adapting, not inventing.

items.who: Walt Disney, as the supposed originator of the mirror rhyme
items.why: The Queen’s question to the glass is in the Grimms’ 1812 first edition ↗ — „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand“ — 125 years before the film. Disney’s contribution was to change it, swapping the doubled ‘mirror’ for ‘Magic Mirror’.

Every English rendering we fetched closes on “fairest of all” — “Who in this land is fairest of all?” ↗ in Ashliman, “Who in this land is the fairest of all?” in Hunt — while the film ends “the fairest one of all.” The smoother “of them all” appears to be pure oral drift.

misattribution.truthLine: The rhyme belongs to Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, first printed in 1812 and usually Englished as “Mirror, mirror, on the wall, / Who in this land is fairest of all? ↗” The film everyone is picturing says something else entirely — “Magic Mirror on the wall” — and the words “of them all” are nobody’s but ours.

context.heading: Why this one drifted
lead: This is the rare misquote where the public remembers a real line — just not from the place they think. Disney’s 1937 Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs is the most-seen Snow White ever made, and its Queen opens with “Magic Mirror on the wall.” But the story Disney adapted had been circulating in English for over a century by then, and in translation after translation the Queen addresses the glass twice over: Spieglein, Spieglein — mirror, mirror.

Memory does the obvious thing: it keeps the more famous picture (Disney’s hooded face in the glass) and the more famous phrasing (the Grimm doublet), and welds them together. Snopes files it under the Mandela effect — a vivid, confidently shared, collectively false memory. The tell is the ending: “who’s the fairest of them all” is smoother than either real line, which is exactly why it won.
context.detailsSummary: The three wordings, side by side
detailsBody: Grimm, German (1812): „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand: wer ist die schönste Frau in dem ganzen Land?“ — trimmed by the 1857 final edition to „Spieglein, Spieglein an der Wand, wer ist die schönste im ganzen Land?“

Grimm, English: Margaret Hunt’s 1884 translation avoids ‘mirror’ entirely — “Looking-glass, Looking-glass, on the wall, Who in this land is the fairest of all?” Modern renderings such as D. L. Ashliman’s give “Mirror, mirror, on the wall, / Who in this land is fairest of all?”
Disney (1937): “Magic Mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?” and, later in the film, “Magic Mirror on the wall, who now is the fairest one of all?”
The popular version: “Mirror, mirror on the wall, who’s the fairest of them all?” — the Grimm opening, the Disney setting, and an ending found in neither.
context.pull: Everyone is quoting a real rhyme — from a book, not a film.
